course.title: AP U.S. History
course.description: Trace how Americans have argued over identity, power, work, and their place in the world, from the societies that existed before 1491 to the present.
course.previewDescription: Follow the nation's development from early contact and colonization through independence, civil war, industrialization, world wars, and recent decades.

unit.title: Period 5
unit.description: Follow Manifest Destiny and the Mexican–American War, the sectional conflict over slavery, the election of 1860 and secession, the Civil War, and Reconstruction and its failure from 1844 to 1877.

topic.title: Failure of Reconstruction
topic.summary: Why freed people stayed poor under sharecropping, how Redeemers, violence, and the Compromise of 1877 ended Reconstruction, and how courts and Southern laws took away African American rights.

framework.name: Course themes
framework.title: Use the course themes to choose your evidence
framework.intro: The themes connect developments across all nine periods. A piece of evidence can fit more than one theme; choose the one that answers the prompt.
framework.sourceNote: Theme names, codes, and descriptions follow the AP U.S. History Course and Exam Description (fall 2026).

themes.title: American and National Identity
themes.description: This theme focuses on how and why definitions of American and national identity and values have developed among the diverse and changing population of North America as well as on related topics, such as citizenship, constitutionalism, foreign policy, assimilation, and American exceptionalism.
themes.question: Who counted as American, and what did people believe the nation stood for?
themes.example: Debates over ratifying the Constitution turned on what kind of republic Americans wanted.

themes.title: Work, Exchange, and Technology
themes.description: This theme focuses on the factors behind the development of systems of economic exchange, particularly the role of technology, economic markets, and government.
themes.question: How did people earn a living, trade, and use new technology?
themes.example: Canals and railroads tied farmers in the West to markets in the East.

themes.title: Geography and the Environment
themes.description: This theme focuses on the role of geography and both the natural and human-made environments in the social and political developments in what would become the United States.
themes.question: How did land, climate, and resources shape choices, and how did people change them?
themes.example: The Chesapeake's climate suited tobacco, which shaped its labor system.

themes.title: Migration and Settlement
themes.description: This theme focuses on why and how the various people who moved to and within the United States both adapted to and transformed their new social and physical environments.
themes.question: Why did people move, and how did they change the places they settled?
themes.example: The Great Migration brought African Americans from the rural South to northern cities.

themes.title: Politics and Power
themes.description: This theme focuses on how different social and political groups have influenced society and government in the United States as well as how political beliefs and institutions have changed over time.
themes.question: Who held power, how did they use it, and who challenged it?
themes.example: The New Deal expanded the federal government's role in the economy.

themes.title: America in the World
themes.description: This theme focuses on the interactions between nations that affected North American history in the colonial period and on the influence of the United States on world affairs.
themes.question: How did contact, trade, diplomacy, and war connect America to other nations?
themes.example: The Seven Years' War left Britain in debt and changed its policies toward the colonies.

themes.title: American and Regional Culture
themes.description: This theme focuses on the how and why national, regional, and group cultures developed and changed as well as how culture has shaped government policy and the economy.
themes.question: How did beliefs, religion, arts, and media develop and shape public life?
themes.example: The Second Great Awakening inspired many Americans to join reform movements.

themes.title: Social Structures
themes.description: This theme focuses on how and why systems of social organization develop and change as well as the impact that these systems have on the broader society.
themes.question: How were people ranked by race, class, and gender, and how did that change?
themes.example: The growth of a middle class in the Gilded Age changed ideas about leisure and family.

questions.prompt: Which of the following describes land ownership in the South after Reconstruction?
choices: Most freed people gained land under Sherman's order and were able to keep it
Planters still held most of the land, and most freed people owned none
The federal government owned most of the farmland and rented it to farmers
Small white farmers held most of the land after the planters had sold their farms
questions.explanation: Planters kept their land, and Congress did not give land to the freed people.
choiceExplanations: Johnson ordered most of the land returned to its former owners.
Planters kept their land, and Congress did not give land to the freed people.
Most farmland remained in private hands.
Planters kept most of their land.
questions.distinguisher: The Sherman's order choice is close because Sherman did set aside land for freed families in 1865, but President Johnson returned most of it to its owners.
questions.subskillText: Identify a historical concept, development, or process.

questions.prompt: Under the sharecropping system, a farm family typically
choices: owned its farm and rented the land to a planter for part of the crop
worked for daily wages paid in cash by the owner of the plantation
worked on land that the government had rented to it at a low cost
worked a plot owned by a landowner in return for a share of the crop
questions.explanation: Sharecropping gave families a plot to farm without cash, but it kept them poor and in debt.
choiceExplanations: Sharecroppers did not own the land.
Sharecroppers were paid with a share of the crop.
The government did not rent land to sharecroppers.
Sharecropping gave families a plot to farm without cash, but it kept them poor and in debt.
questions.distinguisher: The owned its farm choice is close because it also involves a share of the crop, but sharecroppers worked land that belonged to others.
questions.subskillText: Explain a historical concept, development, or process.

questions.prompt: Which of the following helps to explain why many sharecroppers remained in debt?
choices: They bought supplies on credit at high prices, and the debts often exceeded their crops
The federal government taxed their crops more heavily than any other crop
They were paid wages that were too low to allow them to buy a farm
The Freedmen's Bureau charged them high interest on money lent for seed
questions.explanation: Merchants charged high prices on credit, and sharecroppers who could not repay owed the debt into the next year.
choiceExplanations: Merchants charged high prices on credit, and sharecroppers who could not repay owed the debt into the next year.
No such tax existed.
Sharecroppers received a share of the crop and not wages.
The Bureau aimed to help the freed people.
questions.distinguisher: The federal tax choice is close because farmers did pay taxes, but their debts came from credit given by merchants and landowners.
questions.subskillText: Explain how a historical development or process relates to another historical development or process.

questions.prompt: The spread of sharecropping is best understood in the context of which of the following?
choices: A shortage of buyers for cotton in Britain after the Civil War
A federal program that sold farms to freed people at low prices
Freed people who wanted land and planters who had land but little cash
A law that required planters to pay their workers daily wages in cash
questions.explanation: Planters had land but no cash to pay wages, and freed people had labor but no land, so they agreed to share the crop.
choiceExplanations: Cotton continued to be sold abroad.
Congress did not fund any such sale of farms.
Planters had land but no cash to pay wages, and freed people had labor but no land, so they agreed to share the crop.
Planters faced no legal duty to pay cash wages.
questions.distinguisher: The shortage of buyers choice is close because cotton prices fell in later years, but cotton was still sold, and the system arose from a lack of cash and land.
questions.subskillText: Identify and describe a historical context for a specific historical development or process.

questions.prompt: Which of the following helped Redeemers to regain control of Southern state governments?
choices: A federal law that barred Republican officeholders from state governments
The Supreme Court's order for the army to leave the Southern states
The growth of the Republican Party among white landowners in the South
Violence and intimidation against Black voters and Republican officials
questions.explanation: The Klan and similar groups attacked Black voters and Republicans, and fewer people voted as the violence grew.
choiceExplanations: Congress passed no ban on Republican officeholders.
The president withdrew the troops.
Most white Southerners voted for the Democrats.
The Klan and similar groups attacked Black voters and Republicans, and fewer people voted as the violence grew.
questions.distinguisher: The federal law choice is close because Congress did pass laws about officeholders, but the laws it passed protected Black voters and did not remove Republicans.
questions.subskillText: Explain how a historical development or process relates to another historical development or process.

questions.prompt: The Compromise of 1877 is usually described as an arrangement in which
choices: Tilden became president and the army remained in the South for several years
Hayes became president and federal troops were withdrawn from the South
Congress passed a new Civil Rights Act to protect Black voters in the South
Democrats accepted the Reconstruction amendments in return for a lower tariff
questions.explanation: Southern Democrats accepted Hayes's election, and he soon ended the army's presence in the South.
choiceExplanations: Hayes became president.
Southern Democrats accepted Hayes's election, and he soon ended the army's presence in the South.
Federal protection ended.
The arrangement concerned the election and the troops.
questions.distinguisher: The Tilden choice is close because Tilden won the popular vote, but the commission gave the disputed electoral votes to Hayes.
questions.subskillText: Explain a historical concept, development, or process.

questions.prompt: In Plessy v. Ferguson (1896), the Supreme Court
choices: upheld laws that required separate public facilities for Black and white people
ruled that the Fourteenth Amendment barred segregation in public schools
struck down the poll taxes that Southern states used to limit voting
held that Congress could ban discrimination by private businesses
questions.explanation: The Court held that “separate but equal” facilities satisfied the Constitution, which supported segregation for decades.
choiceExplanations: The Court held that “separate but equal” facilities satisfied the Constitution, which supported segregation for decades.
That was the ruling in Brown v. Board of Education (1954).
The Court did not strike down poll taxes in this case.
The Court had rejected that view in 1883.
questions.distinguisher: The Brown choice is close because both cases concerned segregation, but Brown overturned the Plessy rule more than fifty years later.
questions.subskillText: Identify a historical concept, development, or process.

questions.prompt: Which of the following describes a continuity in the South from before the Civil War to the end of Reconstruction?
choices: Black men continued to vote freely and to hold office in large numbers
The federal army continued to enforce civil rights in every Southern state
White landowners kept most of the land and much of the political power
Public schools remained closed and the freed people had no churches
questions.explanation: Slavery had ended, but the planters kept their land, and white Democrats regained control of state governments.
choiceExplanations: Violence and laws pushed them out of politics.
The troops were withdrawn in 1877.
Slavery had ended, but the planters kept their land, and white Democrats regained control of state governments.
Freed people founded schools and churches.
questions.distinguisher: The voting freely choice is close because Black men did vote during Reconstruction, but the gain did not last.
questions.subskillText: Identify patterns among or connections between historical developments and processes.

questions.prompt: Which of the following claims is best supported by the first paragraph of the excerpt?
choices: Hayes held that the South must remain under the army until it became prosperous
Hayes held that Black voters should govern the South until the poverty ended
Hayes held that the South should govern itself and protect the rights of all
Hayes held that the poverty of the South had been caused by federal taxes
questions.explanation: Hayes calls local self-government “the imperative necessity” and says that only a government that “maintains inviolate the rights of all is a true self-government.”
choiceExplanations: He calls for local self-government.
He does not call for rule by one group.
Hayes calls local self-government “the imperative necessity” and says that only a government that “maintains inviolate the rights of all is a true self-government.”
He does not name the cause of the poverty.
questions.distinguisher: The army choice is close because troops were still in some Southern states, but Hayes calls for self-government and not for continued military rule.

stimulusBlocks.source: CED Topic 5.11, KC-5.3.II.E: segregation, violence, Supreme Court decisions, and local political tactics progressively stripped away African American rights
stimulusBlocks.attribution: President Rutherford B. Hayes, in his Inaugural Address on March 5, 1877, after a disputed election and as federal troops were leaving the last Southern states they occupied
stimulusBlocks.citation: Rutherford B. Hayes, Inaugural Address (March 5, 1877). NLTK inaugural corpus, 1877-Hayes.txt.
stimulusBlocks.note: Hayes uses “local self-government” to mean that Southern states would run their own affairs without federal troops. “The white and … the colored people” means white and Black Southerners.
stimulusBlocks.text:
The people of those States are still impoverished, and the inestimable blessing of wise, honest, and peaceful local self-government is not fully enjoyed. Whatever difference of opinion may exist as to the cause of this condition of things, the fact is clear that in the progress of events the time has come when such government is the imperative necessity required by all the varied interests, public and private, of those States. But it must not be forgotten that only a local government which recognizes and maintains inviolate the rights of all is a true self-government.

Let me assure my countrymen of the Southern States that it is my earnest desire to regard and promote their truest interest -- the interests of the white and of the colored people both and equally -- and to put forth my best efforts in behalf of a civil policy which will forever wipe out in our political affairs the color line and the distinction between North and South, to the end that we may have not merely a united North or a united South, but a united country.

questions.subskillText: Identify and describe a claim and/or argument in a text-based or non-text-based source.

questions.prompt: Hayes most likely promised to serve the interests of “the white and of the colored people both and equally” in order to
choices: announce a new program of federal land grants to the freed people
win the confidence of both races while ending federal intervention in Southern affairs
justify the permanent presence of federal troops in the Southern states
ask Congress to remove the governors of the Southern states from office
questions.explanation: Hayes had won a disputed election, and he addressed Southerners of both races as he moved to end federal oversight of the South.
choiceExplanations: The excerpt does not propose land grants.
Hayes had won a disputed election, and he addressed Southerners of both races as he moved to end federal oversight of the South.
He calls for local self-government.
He does not propose removing governors.
questions.distinguisher: The land grants choice is close because the freed people wanted land, but the excerpt makes no such promise.

questions.prompt: Which later development most clearly shows that the promise in the second paragraph was not kept?
choices: The ratification of the Fifteenth Amendment, which protected the vote in 1870
The passage of the Homestead Act, which opened western land to settlers
The purchase of Alaska from Russia during the presidency of Andrew Johnson
Segregation laws and voting limits that took away African Americans' rights
questions.explanation: Hayes spoke of ending “the color line,” but Southern states soon passed Jim Crow laws, poll taxes, and literacy tests.
choiceExplanations: That event came before Hayes's speech.
That law was passed in 1862.
That purchase was made in 1867.
Hayes spoke of ending “the color line,” but Southern states soon passed Jim Crow laws, poll taxes, and literacy tests.
questions.distinguisher: The Fifteenth Amendment choice is close because it concerned rights, but it was ratified in 1870, seven years before Hayes spoke.
